case_info.scenario: A 35-year-old female patient with hypothyroidism and Ehler-Danlos syndrome presented with fatigue, abdominal distension, and dyspnea. She was in good health until 3 weeks prior when she noticed an enlarging nontender right axillary mass. During the previous 2 weeks, she also experienced increasing abdominal distension and indigestion that was worse after food intake. Two days before presentation, she developed dyspnea with exertion. The patient occasionally felt hot but denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her review of systems was negative for chest pain, palpitations, recent sickness contact, or travel. She denied recreational substance use or occupational exposure to carcinogens. She had a relative with breast cancer. On arrival, the patient was afebrile, and her vital signs included a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, oxygen saturation of 94%, and respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory findings showed leukocytosis of 12 400/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001) and an otherwise unremarkable complete blood cell count and basic metabolic panel results. Computed tomography (CT) imaging (Figure 1) revealed bilateral pleural effusions, diffuse gastric wall thickening, extensive lymphadenopathy, and a large right ovarian mass. Pleural fluid analysis from thoracentesis showed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 801 U/L (serum, 865 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]) and protein level of 3.8 g/dL (serum protein, 6 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]). Gram stain results were negative. Additional workup results included a cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) level of 931 U/mL (normal, <46 U/mL [to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1]).
case_info.caption: Coronal view of computerized tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast. The red line illustrates a circumscribed heterogeneous mass from the right ovary measuring 15.4 cm in axial dimension. The yellow 2-sided arrow indicates circumferential thickening of the stomach of up to 2.5 cm. Additional findings included bilateral moderate to large pleural effusion, right axillary lymphadenopathy up to 6.4 cm, and multiple nodular lesions in the peritoneal cavity.
case_info.explanation: A cytology smear is shown inFigure 2. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy of the right axillary lymph node. Planned flow cytometry results showed a monotypic B-cell population that was CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD19-positive, CD20-positive, CD22-positive, CD23-negative, FMC-7–positive, CD38-positive, CD34-negative, and λ light chain–positive. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis indicated fusion ofMYC/IGHin 98% of the cells. Further histological examination showed large-sized B cells that were extensively positive for Epstein-Barr virus and a Ki-67 proliferative rate of greater than 95%. Peripheral blood smear results were negative for malignant cells. The final diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma (BL). Subsequent staging positron emission tomography (PET) CT revealed widespread tracer-avid lesions that were affecting the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, subcarinal, and peritoneal lymph nodes in addition to the involvement of the left breast, left-sided labia, stomach, and ovary. This case highlighted the importance of history taking and laboratory interpretation for the workup of suspected cancer. The abrupt onset and rapid progression suggested a neoplasia characterized by rapid cell growth, a hallmark of aggressive lymphoma that is less common for carcinomas. A Krukenberg tumor denotes a metastatic carcinoma, commonly from a gastrointestinal primary, and presents with synchronous or metachronous ovarian metastasis.1While high-grade carcinomas may exhibit rapid growth, it would be unusual for patients to remain asymptomatic for months leading up to the diagnosis. In contrast, BL, known for its high aggressiveness and rapid proliferation, exhibits a cell doubling time measured in days or even hours.2There are 3 clinical forms of BL: (1) an endemic variant often diagnosed from a large jaw mass in pediatric patients in Africa; (2) an immunodeficiency-associated variant in patients with HIV infection or recipients of organ transplants; and (3) sporadic BL, as in this patient, which often appears with large intraabdominal lesions that affect lymph nodes and solid organs, such as the stomach and ovaries. When approaching a tumor of seemingly unclear primary, it is often tempting to rely on serum tumor markers for diagnosis. This patient had highly elevated levels of CA 125, a widely used biomarker for treatment response monitoring in ovarian cancer. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of CA 125 is limited. In a meta-analysis of 77 studies examining CA 125 levels in patients with a known adnexal mass, the composite sensitivity and specificity were 78% for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.3CA 125, a transmembrane protein, is not reliably produced by some histological subtypes of ovarian tumors. Furthermore, nonmalignant conditions, including menstruation, obesity, and premenopausal status, can be associated with CA 125 levels.4In this patient, CA 125 elevation was indicative of tissue damage by lymphomatous involvement rather than the presence of a primary gynecological neoplasia. The current guidelines by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network underscore the importance of exercising caution when using tumor markers in the diagnostic assessment of tumors without an immediately identifiable primary source.5 After confirming the diagnosis, the patient was promptly transferred to the inpatient hematology service. A tumor lysis panel found elevated uric acid and otherwise normal levels of creatinine, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus. Additional testing included a normal transthoracic echocardiogram and a lumbar puncture with an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Given the acuteness of her presentation, fertility preservation was deferred, and the patient received dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin that was complemented by intrathecal methotrexate. The patient was discharged after receiving her first cycle of chemotherapy. After 2 cycles of treatment, a repeated PET-CT scan indicated the resolution of all lesions except for the residual activity in a right-sided axillary lymph node. After completing all 6 cycles of treatment, restaging PET-CT results showed a complete response, and the patient was transitioned to a surveillance phase.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.caption: Coronal view of computerized tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast. The red line illustrates a circumscribed heterogeneous mass from the right ovary measuring 15.4 cm in axial dimension. The yellow 2-sided arrow indicates circumferential thickening of the stomach of up to 2.5 cm. Additional findings included bilateral moderate to large pleural effusion, right axillary lymphadenopathy up to 6.4 cm, and multiple nodular lesions in the peritoneal cavity.
case_info.explanation: A cytology smear is shown inFigure 2. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy of the right axillary lymph node. Planned flow cytometry results showed a monotypic B-cell population that was CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD19-positive, CD20-positive, CD22-positive, CD23-negative, FMC-7–positive, CD38-positive, CD34-negative, and λ light chain–positive. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis indicated fusion ofMYC/IGHin 98% of the cells. Further histological examination showed large-sized B cells that were extensively positive for Epstein-Barr virus and a Ki-67 proliferative rate of greater than 95%. Peripheral blood smear results were negative for malignant cells. The final diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma (BL). Subsequent staging positron emission tomography (PET) CT revealed widespread tracer-avid lesions that were affecting the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, subcarinal, and peritoneal lymph nodes in addition to the involvement of the left breast, left-sided labia, stomach, and ovary. This case highlighted the importance of history taking and laboratory interpretation for the workup of suspected cancer. The abrupt onset and rapid progression suggested a neoplasia characterized by rapid cell growth, a hallmark of aggressive lymphoma that is less common for carcinomas. A Krukenberg tumor denotes a metastatic carcinoma, commonly from a gastrointestinal primary, and presents with synchronous or metachronous ovarian metastasis.1While high-grade carcinomas may exhibit rapid growth, it would be unusual for patients to remain asymptomatic for months leading up to the diagnosis. In contrast, BL, known for its high aggressiveness and rapid proliferation, exhibits a cell doubling time measured in days or even hours.2There are 3 clinical forms of BL: (1) an endemic variant often diagnosed from a large jaw mass in pediatric patients in Africa; (2) an immunodeficiency-associated variant in patients with HIV infection or recipients of organ transplants; and (3) sporadic BL, as in this patient, which often appears with large intraabdominal lesions that affect lymph nodes and solid organs, such as the stomach and ovaries. When approaching a tumor of seemingly unclear primary, it is often tempting to rely on serum tumor markers for diagnosis. This patient had highly elevated levels of CA 125, a widely used biomarker for treatment response monitoring in ovarian cancer. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of CA 125 is limited. In a meta-analysis of 77 studies examining CA 125 levels in patients with a known adnexal mass, the composite sensitivity and specificity were 78% for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.3CA 125, a transmembrane protein, is not reliably produced by some histological subtypes of ovarian tumors. Furthermore, nonmalignant conditions, including menstruation, obesity, and premenopausal status, can be associated with CA 125 levels.4In this patient, CA 125 elevation was indicative of tissue damage by lymphomatous involvement rather than the presence of a primary gynecological neoplasia. The current guidelines by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network underscore the importance of exercising caution when using tumor markers in the diagnostic assessment of tumors without an immediately identifiable primary source.5 After confirming the diagnosis, the patient was promptly transferred to the inpatient hematology service. A tumor lysis panel found elevated uric acid and otherwise normal levels of creatinine, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus. Additional testing included a normal transthoracic echocardiogram and a lumbar puncture with an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Given the acuteness of her presentation, fertility preservation was deferred, and the patient received dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin that was complemented by intrathecal methotrexate. The patient was discharged after receiving her first cycle of chemotherapy. After 2 cycles of treatment, a repeated PET-CT scan indicated the resolution of all lesions except for the residual activity in a right-sided axillary lymph node. After completing all 6 cycles of treatment, restaging PET-CT results showed a complete response, and the patient was transitioned to a surveillance phase.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

case_info.explanation: A cytology smear is shown inFigure 2. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy of the right axillary lymph node. Planned flow cytometry results showed a monotypic B-cell population that was CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD19-positive, CD20-positive, CD22-positive, CD23-negative, FMC-7–positive, CD38-positive, CD34-negative, and λ light chain–positive. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis indicated fusion ofMYC/IGHin 98% of the cells. Further histological examination showed large-sized B cells that were extensively positive for Epstein-Barr virus and a Ki-67 proliferative rate of greater than 95%. Peripheral blood smear results were negative for malignant cells. The final diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma (BL). Subsequent staging positron emission tomography (PET) CT revealed widespread tracer-avid lesions that were affecting the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, subcarinal, and peritoneal lymph nodes in addition to the involvement of the left breast, left-sided labia, stomach, and ovary. This case highlighted the importance of history taking and laboratory interpretation for the workup of suspected cancer. The abrupt onset and rapid progression suggested a neoplasia characterized by rapid cell growth, a hallmark of aggressive lymphoma that is less common for carcinomas. A Krukenberg tumor denotes a metastatic carcinoma, commonly from a gastrointestinal primary, and presents with synchronous or metachronous ovarian metastasis.1While high-grade carcinomas may exhibit rapid growth, it would be unusual for patients to remain asymptomatic for months leading up to the diagnosis. In contrast, BL, known for its high aggressiveness and rapid proliferation, exhibits a cell doubling time measured in days or even hours.2There are 3 clinical forms of BL: (1) an endemic variant often diagnosed from a large jaw mass in pediatric patients in Africa; (2) an immunodeficiency-associated variant in patients with HIV infection or recipients of organ transplants; and (3) sporadic BL, as in this patient, which often appears with large intraabdominal lesions that affect lymph nodes and solid organs, such as the stomach and ovaries. When approaching a tumor of seemingly unclear primary, it is often tempting to rely on serum tumor markers for diagnosis. This patient had highly elevated levels of CA 125, a widely used biomarker for treatment response monitoring in ovarian cancer. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of CA 125 is limited. In a meta-analysis of 77 studies examining CA 125 levels in patients with a known adnexal mass, the composite sensitivity and specificity were 78% for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.3CA 125, a transmembrane protein, is not reliably produced by some histological subtypes of ovarian tumors. Furthermore, nonmalignant conditions, including menstruation, obesity, and premenopausal status, can be associated with CA 125 levels.4In this patient, CA 125 elevation was indicative of tissue damage by lymphomatous involvement rather than the presence of a primary gynecological neoplasia. The current guidelines by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network underscore the importance of exercising caution when using tumor markers in the diagnostic assessment of tumors without an immediately identifiable primary source.5 After confirming the diagnosis, the patient was promptly transferred to the inpatient hematology service. A tumor lysis panel found elevated uric acid and otherwise normal levels of creatinine, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus. Additional testing included a normal transthoracic echocardiogram and a lumbar puncture with an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Given the acuteness of her presentation, fertility preservation was deferred, and the patient received dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin that was complemented by intrathecal methotrexate. The patient was discharged after receiving her first cycle of chemotherapy. After 2 cycles of treatment, a repeated PET-CT scan indicated the resolution of all lesions except for the residual activity in a right-sided axillary lymph node. After completing all 6 cycles of treatment, restaging PET-CT results showed a complete response, and the patient was transitioned to a surveillance phase.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:

case_info.explanation: A cytology smear is shown inFigure 2. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy of the right axillary lymph node. Planned flow cytometry results showed a monotypic B-cell population that was CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD19-positive, CD20-positive, CD22-positive, CD23-negative, FMC-7–positive, CD38-positive, CD34-negative, and λ light chain–positive. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis indicated fusion ofMYC/IGHin 98% of the cells. Further histological examination showed large-sized B cells that were extensively positive for Epstein-Barr virus and a Ki-67 proliferative rate of greater than 95%. Peripheral blood smear results were negative for malignant cells. The final diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma (BL). Subsequent staging positron emission tomography (PET) CT revealed widespread tracer-avid lesions that were affecting the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, subcarinal, and peritoneal lymph nodes in addition to the involvement of the left breast, left-sided labia, stomach, and ovary. This case highlighted the importance of history taking and laboratory interpretation for the workup of suspected cancer. The abrupt onset and rapid progression suggested a neoplasia characterized by rapid cell growth, a hallmark of aggressive lymphoma that is less common for carcinomas. A Krukenberg tumor denotes a metastatic carcinoma, commonly from a gastrointestinal primary, and presents with synchronous or metachronous ovarian metastasis.1While high-grade carcinomas may exhibit rapid growth, it would be unusual for patients to remain asymptomatic for months leading up to the diagnosis. In contrast, BL, known for its high aggressiveness and rapid proliferation, exhibits a cell doubling time measured in days or even hours.2There are 3 clinical forms of BL: (1) an endemic variant often diagnosed from a large jaw mass in pediatric patients in Africa; (2) an immunodeficiency-associated variant in patients with HIV infection or recipients of organ transplants; and (3) sporadic BL, as in this patient, which often appears with large intraabdominal lesions that affect lymph nodes and solid organs, such as the stomach and ovaries. When approaching a tumor of seemingly unclear primary, it is often tempting to rely on serum tumor markers for diagnosis. This patient had highly elevated levels of CA 125, a widely used biomarker for treatment response monitoring in ovarian cancer. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of CA 125 is limited. In a meta-analysis of 77 studies examining CA 125 levels in patients with a known adnexal mass, the composite sensitivity and specificity were 78% for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.3CA 125, a transmembrane protein, is not reliably produced by some histological subtypes of ovarian tumors. Furthermore, nonmalignant conditions, including menstruation, obesity, and premenopausal status, can be associated with CA 125 levels.4In this patient, CA 125 elevation was indicative of tissue damage by lymphomatous involvement rather than the presence of a primary gynecological neoplasia. The current guidelines by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network underscore the importance of exercising caution when using tumor markers in the diagnostic assessment of tumors without an immediately identifiable primary source.5 After confirming the diagnosis, the patient was promptly transferred to the inpatient hematology service. best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):

case_info.scenario: A 35-year-old female patient with hypothyroidism and Ehler-Danlos syndrome presented with fatigue, abdominal distension, and dyspnea. She was in good health until 3 weeks prior when she noticed an enlarging nontender right axillary mass. During the previous 2 weeks, she also experienced increasing abdominal distension and indigestion that was worse after food intake. Two days before presentation, she developed dyspnea with exertion. The patient occasionally felt hot but denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Her review of systems was negative for chest pain, palpitations, recent sickness contact, or travel. She denied recreational substance use or occupational exposure to carcinogens. She had a relative with breast cancer. On arrival, the patient was afebrile, and her vital signs included a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, oxygen saturation of 94%, and respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute. Laboratory findings showed leukocytosis of 12 400/μL (to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001) and an otherwise unremarkable complete blood cell count and basic metabolic panel results. Computed tomography (CT) imaging (Figure 1) revealed bilateral pleural effusions, diffuse gastric wall thickening, extensive lymphadenopathy, and a large right ovarian mass. Pleural fluid analysis from thoracentesis showed a lactate dehydrogenase level of 801 U/L (serum, 865 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]) and protein level of 3.8 g/dL (serum protein, 6 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]). Gram stain results were negative. Additional workup results included a cancer antigen 125 (CA 125) level of 931 U/mL (normal, <46 U/mL [to convert to kU/L, multiply by 1]).
case_info.caption: Coronal view of computerized tomography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast. The red line illustrates a circumscribed heterogeneous mass from the right ovary measuring 15.4 cm in axial dimension. The yellow 2-sided arrow indicates circumferential thickening of the stomach of up to 2.5 cm. Additional findings included bilateral moderate to large pleural effusion, right axillary lymphadenopathy up to 6.4 cm, and multiple nodular lesions in the peritoneal cavity.
case_info.explanation: A cytology smear is shown inFigure 2. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy of the right axillary lymph node. Planned flow cytometry results showed a monotypic B-cell population that was CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD19-positive, CD20-positive, CD22-positive, CD23-negative, FMC-7–positive, CD38-positive, CD34-negative, and λ light chain–positive. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis indicated fusion ofMYC/IGHin 98% of the cells. Further histological examination showed large-sized B cells that were extensively positive for Epstein-Barr virus and a Ki-67 proliferative rate of greater than 95%. Peripheral blood smear results were negative for malignant cells. The final diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma (BL). Subsequent staging positron emission tomography (PET) CT revealed widespread tracer-avid lesions that were affecting the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, subcarinal, and peritoneal lymph nodes in addition to the involvement of the left breast, left-sided labia, stomach, and ovary. This case highlighted the importance of history taking and laboratory interpretation for the workup of suspected cancer. The abrupt onset and rapid progression suggested a neoplasia characterized by rapid cell growth, a hallmark of aggressive lymphoma that is less common for carcinomas. A Krukenberg tumor denotes a metastatic carcinoma, commonly from a gastrointestinal primary, and presents with synchronous or metachronous ovarian metastasis.1While high-grade carcinomas may exhibit rapid growth, it would be unusual for patients to remain asymptomatic for months leading up to the diagnosis. In contrast, BL, known for its high aggressiveness and rapid proliferation, exhibits a cell doubling time measured in days or even hours.2There are 3 clinical forms of BL: (1) an endemic variant often diagnosed from a large jaw mass in pediatric patients in Africa; (2) an immunodeficiency-associated variant in patients with HIV infection or recipients of organ transplants; and (3) sporadic BL, as in this patient, which often appears with large intraabdominal lesions that affect lymph nodes and solid organs, such as the stomach and ovaries. When approaching a tumor of seemingly unclear primary, it is often tempting to rely on serum tumor markers for diagnosis. This patient had highly elevated levels of CA 125, a widely used biomarker for treatment response monitoring in ovarian cancer. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of CA 125 is limited. In a meta-analysis of 77 studies examining CA 125 levels in patients with a known adnexal mass, the composite sensitivity and specificity were 78% for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.3CA 125, a transmembrane protein, is not reliably produced by some histological subtypes of ovarian tumors. Furthermore, nonmalignant conditions, including menstruation, obesity, and premenopausal status, can be associated with CA 125 levels.4In this patient, CA 125 elevation was indicative of tissue damage by lymphomatous involvement rather than the presence of a primary gynecological neoplasia. The current guidelines by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network underscore the importance of exercising caution when using tumor markers in the diagnostic assessment of tumors without an immediately identifiable primary source.5 After confirming the diagnosis, the patient was promptly transferred to the inpatient hematology service. A tumor lysis panel found elevated uric acid and otherwise normal levels of creatinine, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus. Additional testing included a normal transthoracic echocardiogram and a lumbar puncture with an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Given the acuteness of her presentation, fertility preservation was deferred, and the patient received dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin that was complemented by intrathecal methotrexate. The patient was discharged after receiving her first cycle of chemotherapy. After 2 cycles of treatment, a repeated PET-CT scan indicated the resolution of all lesions except for the residual activity in a right-sided axillary lymph node. After completing all 6 cycles of treatment, restaging PET-CT results showed a complete response, and the patient was transitioned to a surveillance phase.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

case_info.explanation: A cytology smear is shown inFigure 2. The patient underwent an excisional biopsy of the right axillary lymph node. Planned flow cytometry results showed a monotypic B-cell population that was CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD19-positive, CD20-positive, CD22-positive, CD23-negative, FMC-7–positive, CD38-positive, CD34-negative, and λ light chain–positive. Fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis indicated fusion ofMYC/IGHin 98% of the cells. Further histological examination showed large-sized B cells that were extensively positive for Epstein-Barr virus and a Ki-67 proliferative rate of greater than 95%. Peripheral blood smear results were negative for malignant cells. The final diagnosis was Burkitt lymphoma (BL). Subsequent staging positron emission tomography (PET) CT revealed widespread tracer-avid lesions that were affecting the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, subcarinal, and peritoneal lymph nodes in addition to the involvement of the left breast, left-sided labia, stomach, and ovary. This case highlighted the importance of history taking and laboratory interpretation for the workup of suspected cancer. The abrupt onset and rapid progression suggested a neoplasia characterized by rapid cell growth, a hallmark of aggressive lymphoma that is less common for carcinomas. A Krukenberg tumor denotes a metastatic carcinoma, commonly from a gastrointestinal primary, and presents with synchronous or metachronous ovarian metastasis.1While high-grade carcinomas may exhibit rapid growth, it would be unusual for patients to remain asymptomatic for months leading up to the diagnosis. In contrast, BL, known for its high aggressiveness and rapid proliferation, exhibits a cell doubling time measured in days or even hours.2There are 3 clinical forms of BL: (1) an endemic variant often diagnosed from a large jaw mass in pediatric patients in Africa; (2) an immunodeficiency-associated variant in patients with HIV infection or recipients of organ transplants; and (3) sporadic BL, as in this patient, which often appears with large intraabdominal lesions that affect lymph nodes and solid organs, such as the stomach and ovaries. When approaching a tumor of seemingly unclear primary, it is often tempting to rely on serum tumor markers for diagnosis. This patient had highly elevated levels of CA 125, a widely used biomarker for treatment response monitoring in ovarian cancer. Nevertheless, the diagnostic performance of CA 125 is limited. In a meta-analysis of 77 studies examining CA 125 levels in patients with a known adnexal mass, the composite sensitivity and specificity were 78% for the diagnosis of ovarian cancer.3CA 125, a transmembrane protein, is not reliably produced by some histological subtypes of ovarian tumors. Furthermore, nonmalignant conditions, including menstruation, obesity, and premenopausal status, can be associated with CA 125 levels.4In this patient, CA 125 elevation was indicative of tissue damage by lymphomatous involvement rather than the presence of a primary gynecological neoplasia. The current guidelines by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network underscore the importance of exercising caution when using tumor markers in the diagnostic assessment of tumors without an immediately identifiable primary source.5 After confirming the diagnosis, the patient was promptly transferred to the inpatient hematology service. A tumor lysis panel found elevated uric acid and otherwise normal levels of creatinine, calcium, potassium, and phosphorus. Additional testing included a normal transthoracic echocardiogram and a lumbar puncture with an unremarkable cerebrospinal fluid analysis. Given the acuteness of her presentation, fertility preservation was deferred, and the patient received dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin that was complemented by intrathecal methotrexate. The patient was discharged after receiving her first cycle of chemotherapy. After 2 cycles of treatment, a repeated PET-CT scan indicated the resolution of all lesions except for the residual activity in a right-sided axillary lymph node. After completing all 6 cycles of treatment, restaging PET-CT results showed a complete response, and the patient was transitioned to a surveillance phase.
